text:
[RFCS.19.2] **A partial trailing atom ends a `Stream` read incrementally.** In a
`Stream`, a partial trailing atom (a short length or a truncated body) is **EOF, not an
error**, for a reader consuming the stream incrementally: the reader **must** end the
container at the last complete atom ([RFCS.6.6]). A reader whose caller supplied the full
extent — a whole buffer — **may** instead treat a partial trailing atom as an error,
because the caller has asserted that extent is the whole stream; a short tail is then the
caller's slice being wrong, not the stream being in progress.

This clause does not reach a `Dsc`: a truncated `.dsc` is a loader error ([RDSC.9.7]).
Recovery of a crash-truncated recording is the incremental reader's ([RFCS.19.8]).

The two containers share a framing and differ here because of what each is for. A
recording is appended to while it is being read: a reader that called a half-written tail
corruption would fail on every live stream, and [RFCS.19.8]'s recovery to the last complete
atom would have nothing to stand on. A `.dsc` is never appended to while being read. It is a
finished artefact, and a truncated one is a rule bundle missing rules: accepting it would run
a policy the author did not write.

idris.name: Rfcs_19_2__tail_policy
idris.note: What a partial trailing frame means, as an ARGUMENT rather than a constant. This clause gives three answers depending on the container: EOF for a Stream read incrementally, an error a whole-buffer caller MAY raise, and always an error for a Dsc under [RDSC.9.7]. A decoder with one truncation rule cannot be right about both containers, so the caller states which it is.

idris.name: rfcs_19_2__bad_outer_tag_is_not_eof
idris.note: A wrong outer tag is Malformed under EITHER policy. Truncation policy governs a SHORT tail, not a wrong byte -- a reader that treated any frame-level refusal as end-of-stream would accept a corrupt container as a short one, and this clause's EOF rule is about running out of bytes rather than finding the wrong ones.
